title: Nothing to take
hook: no one could enslave Diogenes, because he'd let go of everything they could take

segments.voice: Yesterday: free is wanting rightly, Epictetus' long talk On Freedom. Did you move one want onto the part that was yours? Day four hundred twenty-six.

A pickpocket is working a crowded market. He's good. He reads people by what they clutch: the bag held tight, the hand that keeps checking the back pocket. Then he passes an old man in a torn cloak with an empty bag and a stick, sitting on the steps, laughing at something. The pickpocket walks right by. There is nothing to work with. Epictetus holds this old man, Diogenes, up as a picture of a free person, and he says why, in the middle of that same long talk on freedom. Today: nothing to take.
screen: `A PICKPOCKET READS WHAT YOU CLUTCH.` → `AN OLD MAN WITH AN EMPTY BAG.` → `NOTHING TO TAKE.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. In book four, chapter one, Epictetus says that from the day Diogenes learned from his teacher Antisthenes, no one could make him a slave again. Not because of his birth, not because of a document, but because of how he held things. Second, the handles. Here's a way to see it: everything you own has a handle. Your money has a handle. Your reputation has a handle. Even your body has one. Anyone who wants power over you just grabs the handle you care most about and pulls. In Epictetus' telling, Diogenes held his things so loosely that there was nothing for anyone to grab. Take the cloak, take the bag, even threaten the body: he'd give them up rather than give up himself. Third, the story people tell. Diogenes Laertius, a later collector of stories about the philosophers, says Diogenes was once captured by pirates and put up for sale. Asked what he could do, he said: govern men. Sell me, he said, to someone who needs a master. Nobody knows whether it happened. It's the kind of story that gets told about a person precisely because it fits. Fourth, the honest catch. This isn't a lesson in owning nothing. A life comes with kids, rent and a job, and Epictetus isn't asking anyone to walk away from them. The point is the grip. You can live in a house without being held by it. You can love a reputation without being leashed to it. The question is never how much you have. It's how much of you someone could take by taking it.
screen: `DIOGENES: NOBODY'S SLAVE.` · `EVERYTHING HAS A HANDLE.` · `THE PIRATES AND THE SALE.` · `NOT OWNING NOTHING: THE GRIP.` · then, large: `NOTHING TO TAKE.`

segments.voice: Make a fist with one hand, tight, as if you're holding something you're afraid to lose. Feel the strain in the fingers and the wrist. Name the thing, silently: my phone, my plans, what they think of me. Now slowly open the hand, palm up, and let it rest on your knee. The thing is still yours. You've only changed the grip. Breathe with your hand open. Notice that an open hand can still hold something, and can't be pried. The bell holds the time.
Nothing to take. Epictetus on Diogenes: no one could enslave him, because he held everything loosely enough that there was no handle left to grab. Today's word.
Your line: nothing to take. Pick one thing you grip too hard, a plan, a possession, a role, and loosen your hold on it once today. Day four hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism sometimes rehearse letting go of possessions, roles or reputation in their minds, so that losing them would not mean losing themselves.

fork.setup: you're Diogenes, captured by pirates and standing at the slave market. the auctioneer asks what you can do. what do you say?
options: say you can govern men, and ask to be sold to someone who needs a master.
fork.reveal: in the story told by Diogenes Laertius, he says he can govern men. even on the auction block, there's nothing they can take.

trapdoor: what you thought: freedom means owning a lot.
what it means: Epictetus says Diogenes couldn't be enslaved, because he held his things loosely enough that nothing could be used against him.
what a scholar hears: the pirate-sale story comes from Diogenes Laertius, a later collector, and may be legend rather than history.
